articles.title: This Elementary School Tactic Is a Surefire Way to Make Friends as an Adult (Yes, Really!)
articles.content:
我读小学时，关于丽兹（Liz）的事我知道两件：她的i上头点着气泡，她不会做手撑。第一件是从她课桌上的名牌上看到的，第二件是因为我们在课间花了好几小时互相"教"对方如何倒走。经过一周的摔脸和草污渍后，我把第三件事加进了清单：她成了我最好的朋友。就这么简单。不用"我们什么时候约一约"，不用"我们交换电话"（那时我们连手机都没有），当然也不用为双信是否违反社交规则纠结三天。就像手撑、摔脸、友谊、永远。你也一定有过类似的经历。但成人交朋友可完全是另一回事了。

我做健身教练已经十多年，这让我看到了成人友谊的形成过程。比如，早晨瑜伽班上有两位女士，每周一和三早早来出汗、发抖，还默默咒骂我。她们通常把垫子放在一起。她们能从一排水瓶里认出对方的。她们注意到对方换了新指甲。天哪，她们好几个月来穿得比职业体操运动员还少，却几乎没说过比"早上好"更多的话。

某天，我介绍她们认识，说她们有很多共同点。一阵尴尬的沉默后，其中一人说："看来你也喜欢在破晓前和陌生人在黑暗中受苦。"从那时起，我目睹了她们美好友谊的发展。如今她们一起喝果汁、聊孩子，甚至知道彼此的姓氏。这是我见过无数次的过程：从点头到言语，再到整句，最终形成完整的友谊，包含生日祝福、拼车，整套流程。这可能需要几个月甚至几年——但不必如此。实际上，有一种小学时的交友技巧可以让成人缩短建立关系的时间。我采访了三位友谊专家，他们分享了这个出人意料的简单、略显尴尬但极其有效的技巧，你其实在7岁时就已经掌握，只是后来忘记了。继续往下读，了解这个技巧，你就能更轻松地建立新联系，以各种美好的方式扩大社交圈。

在深入探讨交友技巧之前，我们需要解决一个让人摸不着头脑的社会互动问题：为什么社交随着年龄增长而变化？"成人让交友变得比实际更复杂，"临床心理学家凯勒·舒姆威（Kyler Shumway）博士说，他是《友谊公式》的作者，也是《友谊科学》的主持人。"我们坐等友谊降临，却生活在一个缺乏成人联系结构的世界，随着年龄增长，我们的多样性增加，共同点越来越少。当我们有交友机会时，又小心翼翼，生怕受伤。"

这不仅仅关乎有人在办公室午餐时可坐。"人类有一种基本的心理和生理需求，即与他人建立联系，"埃伦·罗赞斯基（Alan Rozanski）博士说，他是纽约西奈山医学院的医学教授，研究社会联系。他引用了1979年对近7000名成人的一项里程碑式研究，发现社交联系最少的人在研究期间死亡的可能性显著高于社交联系最强的人，无论他们的初始健康状况如何。"之后的每一项研究都证实了这一点。"

准备好了吗？在同一张桌子坐下。对孩子来说，是实际的午餐桌。对成人来说，不必那么字面化，但可以是。我们称之为"午餐桌效应"。它的运作方式是：选择一个地方（跑步俱乐部、妈妈群、健身房、趣味答题夜、戏剧团、拨浆球联盟），定期出现，注意到同样出现的其他人，保持开放态度。最终，这些人会变得熟悉、友好，在稍微脆弱的情况下，成为真正的朋友。"孩子与经常坐在一起的人成为朋友，成人也差不多，"舒姆威说。他解释说，友谊需要三个E：互动、经历和情感结合，分别对应认识新人的机会、共同投入的时间和真实的联系。坐在同一张桌子上几乎自动完成了前两个。

科学支持这一点：美国堪萨斯大学的一项关系研究发现，成人需要大约50小时的共处时间才能从陌生人变成普通朋友，90小时成为真正的朋友，至少200小时才能成为真正亲密的朋友。而90小时基本相当于小学一个学期的课间，200小时略多于一个学年。需要注意的是，不仅仅是时间问题。研究人员发现，在必须的场合（如工作会议或强制性课程）中与人共处的时间，几乎无助于激发友谊。你可以与人共用办公隔间多年，仍然把TA看作"鲍勃，也就是会计部的那个人"。真正重要的是你主动选择的时间。这对儿童来说是通过学校课间、公园和游乐约会自然而然形成的。成人则需要自己创造午餐和课间的版本。

泰勒·梅德（Tayler Meade），一位心理健康教练，著有《致留在草地上走的人》，补充了一个儿童拥有但成人容易失去的相关习惯：留出一个座位。"我们可以开始选择留出座位，无论是象征性还是实际的，"她说，"而不是为我们认为应该联系的人保留座位。"

但坐在同一张桌子只是第一步。某个时刻，必须有人开口说话，这需要一定程度的脆弱，许多成人可能不太习惯。"孩子更愿意脆弱，更愿意展现自己，"罗赞斯基博士说。"对成人来说可能觉得可怕或风险太高，但适当的脆弱是建立互惠关系的方式。"脆弱是实现第三个"E"情感结合的途径。你不必说什么深刻的话，只需说点什么。舒姆威就是个好例子。他分享说，在研究生院，他和同学丹（Dan）在午饭时相处得很好，直到聊天变得尴尬。于是他决定大胆说出来："丹，我要对你真诚脆弱一下。我不太确定怎么交朋友。实际上，我几乎没朋友，也不确定自己会不会。但我喜欢你，你很酷，我想试着和你做朋友。"丹笑了："我刚刚还以为你不喜欢我。"如今，丹是舒姆威最好的朋友、每周健身伙伴，并与他一起演讲关于友谊和神经多样性的主题。

午餐桌效应之所以有效，是因为它解决了成人交友的两个最棘手部分——接近性和时间——同时保持风险相对较低。实际上，你只需要持续出现。怀旧是它的吸引力之一。坐在同一张桌子（或参加同一队伍或同一运动班）让成人回忆起童年时的有趣经历，那时生活简单多了。到成年时期，我们要应对那么多责任，以至于增加一个额外的事情——即使是新朋友——都可能让人感到压力。因此，你需要回到小学水平，罗赞斯基博士说。怎么做？要有意识。这种刻意性非常重要，因为我们优先处理主动选择的事情。"那些重要但不紧急的事，比如朋友，是最容易被推迟到下周的，所以必须有意识地处理它们，"他说。"你需要刻意找到你的‘午餐桌’。"

最后，它的设计是低压力的。你不是在要求任何人成为你的最好朋友，半夜两点送你去机场。你只是邀TA下周一起打拨浆球。然后重复让友谊之路固定下来。每次你出现在熟悉的地方，你的大脑就会把"熟悉人"从"陌生人，可能不安全"类别中移出，重新归类为"可能安全"，这能让你的整个神经系统安定下来。这被称为"单纯接触效应"，即一个非常有名的现象：我们越熟悉某事物（或人），就越喜欢它。因此，每次游戏之夜或瑜伽课上看到同样的面孔，都是你大脑得到的另一次提醒，这些人没问题。共同的积极经历也以其他方式点亮我们的神经通路。罗赞斯基博士指出，一起笑或做有趣的事能激活大脑中的愉悦化学反应，让人们结合。这也是为什么"痛苦爱会聚"类活动（如魔鬼训练、混乱的趣味答题环节、真正糟糕的卡拉OK）能让人们更快产生联结。罗赞斯基博士引用了心理学家丹尼尔·高尔曼（Daniel Goleman）的书《社会智能》，其中详细描述了联系的神经科学，包括镜像神经元——大脑细胞在我们行动时和观察他人行动时都会触发，是我们产生对他人同理心的部分。还有催产素，有时被称作"结合激素"，在积极的社会联系中释放，似乎是人们相互信任的原因之一。但真正的魔力不在于荷尔蒙，而在于重复和一致性，它们训练我们的大脑，平静我们的神经系统。

专家们还有几个简单的技巧，让午餐桌效应更快更有效：

最大的风险不是被拒绝或显得傻气——而是那些在友谊真正开始前就扼杀了它的小错误。午餐桌效应最佳的地方是任何你能定期遇到同一群人的地方。好选择包括：
其中较差的选择是那些设计只为一次互动，之后再无联系的地方：你不主办的婚礼、一次性的社交混合会、音乐会（太吵无法交谈）、或你只认识一个人且对方很快消失的聚会。这些地方没有给午餐桌效应留下任何机会，因为没有"再次相遇"的机会。真正的魔力不在桌子本身，而在于重复访问。因此，下次当你第三个月时与同一位陌生人一起流汗时，不要夸TA的水瓶，而要像舒姆威对丹那样，大胆说出来："嗨，我觉得我们现在应该至少知道彼此的名字了。"最坏的情况是尴尬三秒。最好的情况是，你已经选好了你的桌子。

我们认真核实所有事实和数据，并提供可靠来源，定期更新以确保其准确性。了解我们的团队、贡献者和编辑政策。原文《这个小学时期的技巧能帮你结交成人朋友（真的！）》最初发表于《读者文摘》杂志。

在成人世界，结交朋友似乎比儿时更具挑战性。我们常为工作和家庭事务忙碌，社会圈子也越来越窄。然而，《读者文摘》的专栏作家最近发现，有一个简单的小学技巧可以帮助成年人建立新的友谊——主动邀请他人参与共同活动。

心理学家和社交技巧专家指出，共同体验能有效加深人与人之间的联系。儿童自然地通过游戏、户外活动或手工制作建立友谊，成年人也可以借鉴这一点。研究表明，当人们一起参与有趣或有意义的活动时，更容易建立信任和亲密感。

具体来说，可以从以下几个方面入手：

1. **兴趣小组**：加入或组织与自己爱好相关的活动，如兴趣班、运动俱乐部或志愿者团体。分享共同兴趣是建立友谊的重要基础。
2. **社区活动**：参加社区组织的活动，如节日庆典、公益活动或社区聚会。这些场合提供了认识新朋友的机会。
3. **工作场所**：在职场中主动参与团队活动或组织同事一起吃饭、看电影等。职场关系往往能转化为深厚的友谊。

专家建议，在邀请他人时，最好选择双方都感兴趣的活动，这样更容易打破僵局，建立连接。同时，要保持真诚和耐心，友谊的培养需要时间。

此外，心理学家还强调，社交技巧需要练习和培养。不要害怕尝试，即使面临拒绝或失败，也要保持积极态度。记住，每次互动都是一次学习的机会。

通过这些简单的方法，成年人完全可以像儿童一样轻松结交新朋友，建立有意义的社交关系。
articles.summary:
When I was in elementary school, I knew two things about Liz: She dotted her i’s with bubbles, and she couldn’t do a handstand. The first I learned from the name plate on her desk, and the second because we spent hours during recess trying to “teach” each other how to walk on our hands. After a week of face-plants and grass stains, I added a third thing to my list: She was my best friend. That’s all it took. No “we should hang out sometime,” no “we should exchange numbers” (not like we had phones then anyhow), and certainly no agonizing for three days over whether double-texting is a social crime. It was simply: handstand, face-plant, friendship, forever. 

And you likely have a similar story.

But making friends as an adult is a whole different thing. I’ve been a fitness teacher for more than a decade, which has given me a front-row seat to watching adult friendships form. For example, there were two women in my early morning hot Pilates class who showed up every Monday and Wednesday for months to sweat, shake and silently swear at me. They usually placed their mats next to each other. They could ID the other person’s water bottle in a lineup. They noticed when the other got a new pedicure. Heck, they spent months inches away from each other wearing less clothing than professional gymnasts, and yet they’d never said much beyond “good morning.”

One day, I introduced them, telling them they had a lot in common. There was an awkward silence before one said, “So I see you also like suffering in a dark room with strangers before dawn,” and from that point on, I got to watch a beautiful friendship develop. Now they grab smoothies together, chat about their kids and even know each other’s last names. 

It’s a process I’ve watched dozens of times: going from head nods to words to whole sentences to, eventually, whole friendships, with birthday texts, carpools, the whole shebang. This can take months or even years—but it doesn’t have to. In fact, there’s an elementary school tactic to making friends as an adult that forges those relationships on a truncated timeline. I spoke to three friendship experts about this surprisingly simple, slightly embarrassing, extremely effective technique that you actually mastered by the time you were 7 and just kind of forgot.

Read on to find out what it is so you can make new connections more easily and expand your social circle in all sorts of wonderful ways.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more life hacks, etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

Why is making friends as an adult so much harder?

Before we get into the nitty-gritty of making friends, we need to address this head-scratching part of social interactions and how they change as we get older. “Adults make friendship much harder than it needs to be,” says Kyler Shumway, PsyD, a licensed psychologist who is also the author of The Friendship Formula and the host of Science of Friendship. “We sit around waiting for friendship in a world that lacks structure for adult connection, we age and diversify, and see less and less in common. And then, when we do have opportunities for friendship, we keep our cards close to the chest because we’re afraid of getting burned.”

The stakes here are bigger than just having someone to sit with at lunch in the office. “We have a basic psychological and biological need to be connected to other people,” says Alan Rozanski, MD, a professor of medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who studies social connectivity. He points to research from a landmark 1979 study of nearly 7,000 adults, which found that people with the fewest social ties were significantly more likely to die within the study period than those with the strongest ones, regardless of how healthy they were to begin with. “And every study since has confirmed it.”

What is the elementary school tactic that can help you make friends as an adult?

You ready for this? Sit at the same table. For kids, it’s the actual lunch table. For adults, it doesn’t have to be that literal, although it can be. Let’s call in the Lunch Table Effect. Here’s how it works: Choose one place (a running club, a mom group, a gym, a trivia night, a theater group, a pickleball league), show up consistently, notice the others who are also there, and be open. Eventually, those people become familiar and then friendly and then, with the help of some vulnerability, real friends. 

“Kids become friends with whoever they keep ending up next to, and it’s not that different for adults,” Shumway says. He explains that friendship needs the three E’s: engagement, experience and emotional bonding. Those translate, respectively, to opportunities to meet people, time invested together and some real connection. Sitting at the same table checks off the first two almost automatically.

Science backs this up: A foundational study of relationships done by the University of Kansas found that it takes about 50 hours together for adults to go from strangers to casual friends, 90 hours to become real friends and at least 200 hours to be truly close friends. And guess what—90 hours is basically an elementary school’s semester worth of recess, and 200 is just over a school year.

That said, it’s not just about time. The researchers found that time spent with people in required settings, like a work meeting or a mandatory class, does very little for sparking friendships. You can share a cubicle wall with someone for years and still think of them as “Bob whose middle name is ‘from accounting.’” The hours that truly count are the ones that you actively choose. This is the part that’s built in for children through school recesses, parks and play dates. As an adult, you have to create your own version of lunch and recess. 

Tayler Meade, a mental health coach and the author of A Note to the One Left Walking in the Grass, adds an important related habit kids have that adults tend to lose: They leave a seat open. “We can start choosing to leave seats open, metaphorically and physically,” she says, “instead of saving them for people we think we’re supposed to connect with.”

But sitting at the same table is just the first step. At some point, someone is going to have to say something, and this requires a measure of vulnerability that many adults are not comfortable with. “Kids are naturally more willing to be vulnerable, to put themselves out there,” Dr. Rozanski says. “It can feel scary or too risky to adults, but offering a little vulnerability is how we build reciprocal relationships.” Vulnerability is how you get to the third “E”: emotional bonding. 

You don’t have to say anything profound; you just have to say something. Shumway is a good example of how this works. He shares that in grad school, he’d been hitting it off with a classmate named Dan over lunch, until the conversation ran dry and things got awkwardly quiet. So he decided to just say the thing out loud: “Dan, I’m going to try to be real vulnerable with you. I’m not really sure how to make a friend. I don’t have any, really, and I’m not sure if I know how. But I like you, you’re a cool dude, and I want to try to be friends with you.” Dan grinned. “I was just starting to think you didn’t like me,” he said. Dan is now Shumway’s best friend, weekly workout buddy and co-speaker on friendship and neurodiversity.

Why does the Lunch Table Effect work so well?

The Lunch Table Effect works because it solves two of the trickiest parts of making adult friends—proximity and time—while keeping things relatively low stakes. Really, all you need to do is keep showing up. 

Nostalgia is a big part of the appeal. Sitting at the same table (or being on the same team or in the same exercise class) reminds adults of the fun things they used to do when they were kids, when life felt simpler. By the time you’re an adult, you’re juggling so many responsibilities that the thought of adding one extra thing—even if that is a new friend—can feel overwhelming. So you need to take it back to the primary school level, Dr. Rozanski says. 

How do you do that? By being deliberate. This intentionality is super important because you prioritize things that you actively choose. “Things that are important but not urgent, like friends, are the easiest things to bump to next week, so you have to be intentional about it,” he explains. “You need to intentionally find your ‘lunch table.’” 

And lastly, it’s low pressure by design. You’re not asking anyone to be your best friend and drive you to the airport at 2 a.m. You’re just asking them to play pickleball next week. Then the repetition locks in the path to friendship.

What happens in our brains when we do this?

Every time you show up somewhere familiar, your brain takes familiar people from the “stranger, therefore possibly unsafe” category and reclassifies them as “probably safe,” which settles down your whole nervous system. It’s called the mere-exposure effect, the well-documented phenomenon that the more familiar things (and people) become, the more we like them. So every game night or yoga class where you see the same faces is another reinforcement to your brain that these people are OK.

Shared positive experiences also light up our neural pathways in ways that other things don’t. Dr. Rozanski points out that laughing or doing something enjoyable together triggers the feel-good brain chemistry that bonds people. And it’s one reason why “misery loves company” activities (a killer workout, a chaotic trivia round, truly bad karaoke) tend to bond people even faster. Dr. Rozanski references psychologist Daniel Goleman’s book Social Intelligence, which details the neuroscience of connection, including mirror neurons—brain cells that fire both when we act and when we watch someone else act, part of how we come to feel empathy for others. And oxytocin, sometimes nicknamed the “bonding hormone,” is released during positive social connections and seems to be part of what causes people to trust each other. 

But the real magic isn’t the hormones, he says. It’s in the repetition and consistency, which trains our brains and calms our nervous system.

What will give this a higher probability of success?

Our experts have a few simple tips to make the Lunch Table Effect work faster and more effectively:

  • Put cheese on the broccoli. “Social interaction can feel a lot like broccoli,” Shumway says. “We know it’s healthy and good for us, but it’s not always appealing.” His fix: Pick a “table” you’d enjoy sitting at, even if you never made a single friend there. Like moving? Try a climbing gym or hiking group. Like reading? Join a book club. Can’t find a group that fits? Start one. Shumway runs a recurring D&D game wherever he lives because he genuinely loves it, friends or no friends. 
  • Skip the small talk (once you’ve earned the right to). Once you’ve become acquaintances, skip past the “some weather we’re having” for a line with more substance, like: “What’s something you’re really excited about this week?” People consistently underestimate how much they’ll enjoy a deeper conversation even with someone they barely know, and they tend to feel happier and more connected than if they stuck to small talk. 
  • Say hi to everyone, not just your favorite person. Meade is big on this one. The more you look around for others to include, the more potential friends you will find, even if they’re not the ones you’d usually think of first. Even brief interactions make you feel happier, and practicing on low-stakes strangers makes the real invitations feel easier.
  • Move away from the table eventually. The table is great for establishing a relationship, but true friendships evolve past one single activity. Remember, hours spent purely inside one closed system don’t build closeness on their own—the relationship needs proof it can survive outside its original habitat.
  • Schedule it. Yes, on your actual calendar. Because friendship falls into that “important but not urgent” quadrant, Dr. Rozanski suggests deciding in advance how often you’ll show up—weekly, twice a month, whatever—instead of leaving it to whenever you happen to feel like it.
  • Give it at least three tries. Too many adults go to one dance class, don’t make a friend, then give up and go home. Or they’ll have a small rough patch and decide the other person isn’t worth it. But kids don’t give up after the first try, and “they can disagree during playtime and hug at the end of the day,” Meade says. Adults tend to treat one awkward interaction as a final verdict. Shumway’s rule of thumb: Try connecting three times before reading it as a genuine no.

What mistakes should you avoid?

The biggest risks here aren’t rejection or looking silly—they’re the little mistakes that torpedo the friendship before it can really get going.

  • Don’t assume proximity is enough. If your only shared “table” is a required one, then pick a chosen activity on top of it—lunch away from your desk, happy hour, anything you’re both there for by choice.
  • Don’t be glued to your phone. Dr. Rozanski describes how people used to talk to their neighbors on the bus, and now, everyone is on their phones. But every scroll is a small, missed opportunity for a connection. And this includes taking out your earbuds if you’re used to wearing them everywhere.
  • Don’t resort to gossip. A common friendship mistake is to “bond” over talking about others. “Those are empty calories,” Dr. Rozanski says, referring to quick, easy chatter about other people, as opposed to “the stuff that fills us up,” which comes from actually giving something of yourself. Not only that, but gossip can backfire by making you look less trustworthy.
  • Don’t mask. Kids haven’t yet learned to mask out of fear of shame or rejection, so they’ll tell a total stranger they like their shirt, or that their dog just died, within minutes of meeting them. Shumway says adults tend to do the opposite, presenting a safe, buttoned-up version instead. Closeness comes from being willing to be seen, not from being impressive.

Where might you have the most luck with this technique?

The optimal places for the Lunch Table Effect are anywhere that you’d see the same people consistently. Good bets include:

  • A recurring class you’d enjoy anyway—dance, spin, pottery, improv, a language course
  • An athletic group, like a running club, rec league or regular pickup game
  • Trivia night, or a bar that hosts the same event weekly
  • Volunteering for a cause you genuinely care about
  • A book club, hobby group or recurring tabletop game
  • A place of worship or community group you attend regularly
  • The dog park at roughly the same time each day

Worse bets are the places designed for exactly one interaction and then never again: a wedding you’re not hosting, a one-off networking mixer, a concert (too loud to actually talk), or a party where you know exactly one other person who promptly disappears. None of those gives the Lunch Table Effect anything to work with, because there’s no “again” built in. The magic sauce isn’t the table itself. It’s the repeat visit.

So the next time you’re sweating next to the same stranger for the third month in a row, skip the compliment about their water bottle and instead try what Shumway did with Dan and just say the thing: “Hey, I feel like we should actually know each other’s names by now.” Worst case, it’s a little embarrassing for three seconds. Best case, you’ve just picked your table.

He is the author of The Friendship Formula and has written and spoken widely on friendship, mental health and neurodiversity, including in the Audible Original series Science of Friendship.

articles.title: 17 Accidental Gen Alpha Insults That Will Make You Feel Really Old (Seriously, Ouch)
articles.content:
1953年，彩色电视问世。你我出生时它已存在多年。可如今，一个从4K HDR时代成长起来的孩子却问你童年时是否看过彩色电视。他们并非完全无理——毕竟他们的祖父母确实曾看过黑白电视，而你在他们眼中同样古老。此刻，你可以打电话给妈妈，告诉她你终于理解当年她被问及是否认识亚伯拉罕·林肯时的感受了。

这需要一点背景说明：孩子并非在嫌你太老。他们只是被你的年龄所震惊，无论你是42岁、51岁还是36岁。对一个9岁的孩子来说，这些数字代表的是难以想象的漫长岁月——你的生命几乎相当于他们四倍。在他们的算术里，你简直是耐力的奇迹。我得说，衰老从未如此美好（尽管他们不这么想）。

这首歌并不重要。无论是你22岁时的热门流行曲、一路走过的慢摇、依然热爱的金曲，还是曾与朋友穿着毅力底裤（带毛！）跳过的臀部舞曲——这首歌现在也出现在了祖母的播放列表中，孩子们因此建立了这层联系。

顺便说一句，这并非对你的评判，而是对祖母们美妙品味的致敬。这将是你下午自言自语的故事。

最残忍的是，被提及的物品并非复古。它不是怀旧款，也不是二手店淘来的。你最近在商店用钱买的，觉得设计不错。Gen Alpha（Z世代）对时尚的理解被2000年代早期的"复古风"所定义，这意味着你年轻时的衣橱如今成了潮流，而低腰牛仔裤的回归更是噩梦重现。（见："我爷爷也有这件衬衫！"）

蓝色牛仔裤的争议已广为人知，但当一个孩子将你整个青春或早期成人阶段的穿衣风格视为戏装时，你完全无法准备。当年这些不是复古款，只是普通牛仔裤。如今它们重回流行，意味着你见证了时尚的完整革命周期，这是一种你未曾请求的"荣誉"。

2006年，冥王星被降级为矮行星。如果你在2006年前上学，你学习、背诵、制作太阳系模型，甚至考试时都有九大行星。你以为这是定论。然而，一个只知八大行星的孩子现在正用耐心关切的眼神看着你，就像你看待仍认为地球是太阳系中心的人一样。我们学错了，且永远无法彻底纠正。

Gen Alpha（Z世代）已经有了精心设计的护肤步骤和美妆购物清单，你会以为他们更懂自己要预防什么。然而，我的侄女在仔细研究我的脸后，震惊地发现笑纹不是动画中快乐角色脸颊上的漫画线条，而是多年来微笑后真正刻在脸上的痕迹。她逐一指给我看。但拥有笑纹也棒极了，因为这意味着你人生中笑过很多次……对吧？

解释上世纪90年代末到21世纪初的"狂刷眉毛风潮"简直无法体面。我们将眉毛狂刷成细若线条的弧形，然后用笔画回一部分。没错，我们以为这样很美。我的Gwen Stefani海报就是证明。如今，Gen Alpha（Z世代）——在浓密自然的眉毛审美中长大的一代——看见你的年鉴照片后，都以为我们患了某种怪病。

最糟的是，我们刷到现在，许多人眉毛仍有秃疤。谢谢你了，Gwen！

这个问题自带矛盾，孩子们却没发现。虽然有"谷歌前"时代（谷歌1998年推出，但几年后才成为所有人的首选），但"谷歌前"并没有谷歌。那时只有纸张。你在百科全书里查资料，或者从图书馆借书，先在卡片目录中查找，再用杜威十进制分类法定位。可能还会与兄弟姐妹争执不休。或者，坦白说，你可能根本不知道答案，然后继续过日子。谷歌前的版本就是不确定性，而我们曾习惯那种生活。

我的手机亮度基本全开，否则看不清小字！同样，我丈夫放大的文字几乎是一字一行地发来。当孩子问你这个问题时，你不得不面对眼睛已不如从前的现实。这终将发生在他们身上，但可能要30年后，届时某个Gen Beta（Y世代）的孩子也会问同样问题，循环重启。

令你更糟心的是，你高中甚至大学才有自己的手机。然后还得告诉孩子，在此之前，家里只有一个座机（没错，一户一个电话号码），别人要联系你必须先打到家里，和你的父母说话。

对Gen Alpha（Z世代）来说，手机和平板就像鞋子一样基本。没有这些就像缺氧。同样，我的孩子问我为什么手机号是明尼苏达州的编号时，我解释当年电话号码与地点绑定，搬家就换号。直到某天我们决定永远保留手机号，而我恰好那天住在明尼苏达州。

我最近试图向朋友三年级的孩子解释"任期电视"，但最终放弃了，因为他们完全不理解。首先，电视不便携。虽然你可以换台（需查物理杂志《电视指南》确认播出时间），但必须看完整节目，不能跳过。这要求你在特定时间、正确频道、在家里、在兄弟姐妹前准时到场，否则错过节目，重播极少。

但我高中最美好的回忆之一就是每周四晚上8点与朋友看《老友记》。

当年在超市省钱需要实体剪刀、周日报纸和小小的组织系统。优惠券放在信封或小折叠文件夹里。还要检查到期时间。这是一项完整的活动。事实上，这曾是一种流行的爱好，甚至有专门的电视节目。然而，Gen Alpha（Z世代）——他们结账时轻点手机无需抬头——将其视为与自制黄油无异的古怪行为。

Gen Alpha（Z世代）有自己的数字生活词汇，但语音留言不在其中。语音留言是在打电话未接通时，用声音代替正常的短信，录制一段语音，收件人会因此感到轻微焦虑，3-5个工作日后才能听到（如果信箱还能收信，没满的话）。对一个完全靠语音备忘录和短信交流的孩子来说，这个区别完全不懂。别提那些连接在电话上的独立留言机，用实体磁带录音的了。简直可怕！

现金是古迹。分币已停用，5分币可能也快了。但这不重要，因为没人再用现金，更不用说硬币了。然而曾经有一段时间，硬币如此珍贵，我们有专门的罐子、钱包、猪猪筐、碟子、裤兜和车载装置存放它们。或许你现在仍有几个装满零钱的罐子，多年交易的余额积累。但要知道，Gen Alpha（Z世代）被你的古物罐子困惑了。他们不理解你为什么要存它，打算怎么用它，或者为什么不直接刷卡。将零钱卷起来存进银行的故事，可以留到他们长大需要理解痛苦时再讲。

智能手机前，你必须记住电话号码——最好朋友的、祖父母的、披萨店的、自己的，甚至几个前男友的号码（令人尴尬地，它们仍存在记忆深处）。这是生存技能。Gen Alpha（Z世代）觉得这很诡异，就像发现你能用回声定位。为什么大脑要刻意记住电话号码？为了什么？他们可能连自己的号码都不知道。

现今全球仅剩三家Blockbuster（百视达）影碟店，其中一家在俄勒冈州本德市，人们前去参观如同朝圣。因此，提到这家店或租碟的概念，孩子感到困惑也合情合理。他们从未体验过：驱车去店租碟、看完后倒带、按时归还或缴纳高额逾期费用，以及到店发现想看的电影已被别人先借走的无助愤怒。在这一点上，他们是幸运的。

别担心。Gen Beta（Y世代）已经来临，他们将是我们的复仇！
articles.summary:
“Was color TV around when you were a kid?”

Color television was invented in 1953. You and I were born well after that. And yet here is a child, whose entire visual life has been 4K HDR, asking whether you experienced colors as a child. They’re not entirely off base in their reasoning—their grandparents did grow up with black-and-white TV, and you are, to them, also old. What you can do now is call your mom and tell her you finally understand how she felt when you asked her if she knew Abraham Lincoln personally.

“Wow, people live that long?”

This one requires context: The child is not reacting to an advanced age. They are reacting to your age, whatever it is. Forty-two. Fifty-one. Thirty-six. To a 9-year-old, all of these numbers represent a span of time so vast, it is barely comprehensible. You have been alive for basically their entire lifespan four times over. You are, by their math, a marvel of endurance. And I have to say that getting older has never looked so good (no matter what they think).

“My grandma loves that song too!”

The song does not matter. Whatever song it is—a pop hit you loved at 22, a slow jam you played on a road trip, a banger you still consider current, a bootylicious bop that you and your friends would drop it low to while wearing your apple-bottom jeans (with the fur!)—it has also found its way into a grandmother’s playlist, and this child has now connected those two data points.

For the record, this says nothing about you and everything about grandmothers having excellent taste. This is the story you will be telling yourself for the rest of the afternoon.

“Is that what people wore back then?”

The particular cruelty of this one is that the item in question is not vintage. It is not a throwback. It did not come from a thrift store. You bought it recently, at a store, with money, because you thought it looked nice. Gen Alpha’s relationship with fashion is complicated by the fact that they are currently obsessed with “vintage Y2K” looks—which is to say, your early-2000s wardrobe is now a vibe, and the threat of low-rise jeans returning is a horrifying reality. (See also: “My grandpa has that same shirt!”)

“Check out my retro skinny jeans!”

The skinny-jean drama has been well documented, but nothing prepares you for the moment a child presents your entire adolescent or early-adult wardrobe as a costume. These were not vintage when you wore them. These were just jeans. The fact that they have now lapped the trend cycle and returned as “retro” means that you are old enough to have personally witnessed a complete revolution of fashion, and that is an honor no one asked for.

“There aren’t nine planets in our solar system.”

Pluto was demoted from being a planet in 2006. If you went to school before 2006, you learned nine planets, memorized nine planets, made a solar system mobile with nine planets and took tests about the nine planets. You thought it was settled science. It was not settled. And now a child who has only ever known eight planets is looking at you with patient concern, the way you’d look at someone who still thought the Earth was the center of the solar system. We were taught this wrong, and we will never fully recover.

“Oh, that’s what smile lines are!”

Gen Alpha already has elaborate skin-care routines and Sephora hauls, so you’d think they’d have a better grasp of what they’re actually trying to prevent. And yet my niece was shocked to learn that smile lines aren’t the cartoon lines over a happy character’s cheeks in anime, but real lines that get etched into a person’s face after years of smiling. She learned that after very closely examining my face and pointing out the lines one by one. But hey, having smile lines is a gift because it means you’ve done a lot of smiling in your life … right?

“Why are your eyebrows so thin in that picture?”

There is no graceful way to explain the Great Eyebrow Purge of the late 1990s and early 2000s. We aggressively plucked them into a thin, slightly surprised arch that we then partially drew back on with a pencil. Yes, we thought this looked good. My Gwen Stefani poster proved it. And now Gen Alpha—a generation that has grown up worshiping full, natural, bushy brows as the beauty ideal—is looking at your yearbook pictures and wondering what weird eyebrow disease we all had.

The worst part? We plucked our brows so much that many of us still have bald patches. Thanks for nothing, Gwen.

“What did you Google on before Google?”

The question contains its own paradox, which kids do not notice. While there was a “before Google” (it launched in 1998 but did not become everyone’s first stop for everything until several years later), there was no “Google” before Google. There was just paper. As in, you looked things up in an encyclopedia. Or sometimes in books that you had to physically get from a library after looking them up in the card catalog and locating by using the Dewey decimal system. Maybe you argued with your older siblings about it. Or, if we’re being really honest, you just didn’t know the thing and went about your day. The earlier version of Google was uncertainty, and we just lived with it.

“Why is the text on your screen so big and bright?”

My phone is set to max brightness pretty much all the time. I can’t see the tiny type otherwise! Similarly, my husband has his text so enlarged that his texts basically come in one letter at a time. So when your kid asks you this, you’re forced to confront the reality that your eyes are not what they used to be. This will certainly happen to them someday but probably not for another 30 years, at which point some Gen Beta child will ask them the same question and the cycle will be complete.

“How old were you when your parents let you have a phone?”

It was bad enough that you didn’t have a personal cellphone until high school or possibly college. But then you have to tell your kids that before that, there was a house phone (yes, only one phone number per house) and that if someone wanted to reach you, they called your home and talked to your parents first.

For Gen Alpha, a phone or tablet is as basic as shoes. The idea of not having one is akin to not having oxygen. Similarly, my kids have asked me why my phone number has a Minnesota area code, and it was a bit surreal explaining to them that the phone number used to be attached to a location and when you moved you got a new one. Until one day we all just decided to keep our phone numbers forever, and I happened to be living in Minnesota that day.

“Why did you have to be home to watch TV?”

I tried to explain appointment television to a friend’s third-grader recently and eventually gave up because they couldn’t grasp any part of what I was saying. First, TVs weren’t portable. And sure, you could change the channel (after looking up the showtime in a physical magazine called the TV Guide), but then you had to watch whatever was playing. To the end with no skipping. And all of this required you to be home, in person, at a precise time (before your brother) and on the correct channel. Otherwise, you missed your show, and there were rarely replays.

Still, some of my fondest high school memories involve sitting down at 8 p.m. every Thursday to watch Friends with my friends.

“What does ‘clipping a coupon’ mean?”

There was a time when saving money at the grocery store required physical scissors, a Sunday newspaper and a small organizational system. The coupons lived in an envelope or a little accordion folder. You checked expiration dates. It was an entire activity. In fact, it was so popular as a hobby that there were entire TV shows about it. Yet Gen Alpha, who taps-to-save at checkout without looking up from their screen, finds this functionally indistinguishable from churning your own butter.

“What’s a voicemail?”

Gen Alpha has its own rich vocabulary for digital life, but voicemail is not in it. Voicemail is what happens when you call someone and they don’t answer, and instead of texting like a normal person, you leave a recording of your voice that the recipient will then feel mildly anxious about for three to five business days before listening to it. (If their mailbox is even accepting new messages and isn’t full.)

To a child who communicates entirely in voice memos and texts, this distinction is simply lost. And don’t even get started on the voicemails left on a separate machine that you attached to your phone and recorded on physical tapes. The horror!

“Why do you put your change in a jar?”

Cash is a relic. Pennies have been discontinued, and nickels probably will soon follow. But it doesn’t matter because no one uses cash anymore, much less coins. But there was a time when coins were so precious that we had special jars, purses, piggy banks, dishes, pants pockets and car doohickeys for storing them. Maybe you still have the jar of change on your dresser, accumulated over years of transactions that didn’t end in an even number.

But just know that Gen Alpha is baffled by your jar of relics. They do not understand why you have it, what you plan to do with it or why you didn’t just tap. Rolling coins to take to the bank is a story you can save for when they’re older and need to understand suffering.

“Why do you have my phone number memorized?”

Before smartphones, you memorized phone numbers—your best friend’s number, your grandparents’ number, the number for the pizza place, your own number, several ex-boyfriends’ numbers (that you still, embarrassingly, have stored somewhere up there). You had to. It was a survival skill.

Gen Alpha finds this deeply weird, like discovering you can echolocate. Why would a brain hold phone numbers on purpose? For what? Chances are, they don’t even know their own phone number.

“What’s a Blockbuster?”

There are now three Blockbuster locations left in the entire world. One of them is in Bend, Oregon, and people visit it the way they visit national monuments. So it’s understandable why a child would be confused if you mention the word or anything about holding videos in your hands. The child asking you this question has never experienced the specific ritual of driving to a store to rent a physical object, rewinding it when you were done, returning it on time or paying a genuinely unreasonable late fee, and arriving to discover that the movie you wanted was already gone because someone else got there first. They will never know that particular helpless fury. In some ways, they are the lucky ones.

Don’t worry, though. Gen Beta is already here, and they will be our revenge!

articles.title: Brace Yourself! You’re About to Get a Lot More Political Fundraising Emails Before the Midterms—Here’s Why and What to Do About It
articles.content:
In a democracy, elections are our collective voice—even if, in our specific democracy, the loudest voices seem to be a bunch of email marketers. That’s going to be especially apparent this midterm season, which is well underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Warm up that delete finger, because it will be getting a workout.
Why? Well, just when you thought your inbox couldn’t get any more stuffed with stuff you don’t want to read, a major email carrier recently launched new fundraising rules for political groups. And you can be certain they will take advantage of them. How much can possibly fit into our already-at-capacity inboxes? Just you wait. Things are about to get way worse—but there is something you can do about it. Read on for the details.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Google recently launched a new Gmail Verified Sender Program, which will allow “eligible, verified political committees” to send “policy-compliant and non-abusive messages” straight to your email inbox, bypassing the spam filter.
The program is open to candidates, political parties, political action committees (PACs) and similar groups registered with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) or other election authorities. To qualify, political senders must be verified, send emails from a public domain and keep spam below 0.3% of the total number of email they send. If users mark more than 0.3% as spam when the emails come in, senders can get suspended for seven days or booted from the program.
The policy went into effect on Sept. 8, so the new reality is well underway.
One reason Google may have decided to allow increased political fundraising is to reduce the number of lawsuits it’s had to respond to. The Republican National Committee (RNC) sued Google in 2022 for “throttling” its email messaging campaigns with its spam filters. The case was dismissed, but the RNC appealed. In January 2026, the RNC lost again.
Also in 2022, the RNC and the Republican Senate and Congressional campaign committees filed a joint complaint with the FEC over Google’s spam filters, which they accused of intentionally censoring their messages. The FEC dismissed the complaint. Other lawsuits and complaints over the years have met similar fates.
But back to the original question. Given the lack of a big announcement by the company, it’s not clear that Google does think it’s a good idea, at least in terms of pleasing Gmail recipients. Google quietly updated its Help Center website to reflect the policy change, underscoring the idea that it anticipates users will not be happy with the increased email traffic.
And this isn’t the first time Google tried this. Back in 2022, the company launched a pilot program that also prevented political emails from being filtered as spam. Comments to the FEC were uniformly negative, according to a review of hundreds of them by Axios.
The main one has less to do with the volume of spam and more with the senders themselves. Being verified under this program doesn’t tell you anything about the fundraisers’ business practices or where your money will go.

In a democracy, elections are our collective voice—even if, in our specific democracy, the loudest voices seem to be a bunch of email marketers. That’s going to be especially apparent this midterm season, which is well underway ahead of the Nov. 3 election. Warm up that delete finger, because it will be getting a workout.

Why? Well, just when you thought your inbox couldn’t get any more stuffed with stuff you don’t want to read, a major email carrier recently launched new fundraising rules for political groups. And you can be certain they will take advantage of them. How much can possibly fit into our already-at-capacity inboxes? Just you wait. Things are about to get way worse—but there is something you can do about it. Read on for the details.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.

Why are we about to get an avalanche of political fundraising emails?

Google recently launched a new Gmail Verified Sender Program, which will allow “eligible, verified political committees” to send “policy-compliant and non-abusive messages” straight to your email inbox, bypassing the spam filter.

The program is open to candidates, political parties, political action committees (PACs) and similar groups registered with the Federal Election Commission (FEC) or other election authorities. To qualify, political senders must be verified, send emails from a public domain and keep spam below 0.3% of the total number of email they send. If users mark more than 0.3% as spam when the emails come in, senders can get suspended for seven days or booted from the program.

The policy went into effect on Sept. 8, so the new reality is well underway.

Why did Google think this was a good idea?

One reason Google may have decided to allow increased political fundraising is to reduce the number of lawsuits it’s had to respond to. The Republican National Committee (RNC) sued Google in 2022 for “throttling” its email messaging campaigns with its spam filters. The case was dismissed, but the RNC appealed. In January 2026, the RNC lost again.

Also in 2022, the RNC and the Republican Senate and Congressional campaign committees filed a joint complaint with the FEC over Google’s spam filters, which they accused of intentionally censoring their messages. The FEC dismissed the complaint. Other lawsuits and complaints over the years have met similar fates.

But back to the original question. Given the lack of a big announcement by the company, it’s not clear that Google does think it’s a good idea, at least in terms of pleasing Gmail recipients. Google quietly updated its Help Center website to reflect the policy change, underscoring the idea that it anticipates users will not be happy with the increased email traffic.

And this isn’t the first time Google tried this. Back in 2022, the company launched a pilot program that also prevented political emails from being filtered as spam. Comments to the FEC were uniformly negative, according to a review of hundreds of them by Axios.

Aside from an overflowing inbox, are there any other potential dangers?

The main one has less to do with the volume of spam and more with the senders themselves. Being verified under this program doesn’t tell you anything about the fundraisers’ business practices or where your money will go.

“I did a lot of work in Congress to crack down on scam PACs that send you fundraising,” Katie Porter, a former Democratic congresswoman from California, told CNN when the policy became public. “They say they’re going to help elect veterans, but when you look at where the money goes, 99.99% of the money goes back into the pockets of political consultants. This doesn’t do anything to tackle that.”

Another risk is scammers trying to mimic a legitimate political group to solicit funds, harvest your data or hack your accounts. In 2021, the Department of Justice (DOJ) charged three people with fraudulently soliciting $3.5 million from unsuspecting givers. And just before the 2024 election, the FBI warned of phishing scams, merchandise “no-shipment” scams and other fraudulent activity masked as legitimate political correspondence.

Is there any way to stop the deluge of emails?

You can reduce them, but it’s unlikely you can stop them completely. Here are four options.

  • Click unsubscribe. Google recommends that senders offer a one-click unsubscribe button, so use it. You can also open the message and navigate to the unsubscribe options at the company’s website.
  • Create a filter. In the search bar at the top, click the “show search options” icon to show filters. Or click the box next to an unwanted email, then hit the three dots menu and select “filter messages like these.”
  • Mark the email as spam. If a company does not unsubscribe you, mark the emails as spam. Know that this will not unsubscribe you, but it will send the emails automatically to your spam inbox.
  • Block the sender. If you want nothing else from the sender at all, open the email, hit the three dots “more” menu and select “Block [sender].”

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Josh Groban Keeps Leveling Up—And His Next Chapter Might Be His Most Ambitious Yet
articles.content:
当约什·格罗班推出新专辑《Cinematic》时，这似乎理所当然，因为他的成功故事本身就像电影情节：一个焦虑的少年在学校难以专注，加入合唱团（并发现自己在唱歌方面相当出色），在声乐教练的指导下，17岁时与格莱美奖获奖制作人大卫·福斯特合作，并最终与席琳·迪翁同台表演。然后……名利双收，幸福永远，对吧？"嗯，"格罗班在我们5月的一个温暖的日子在纽约坐下时面露羞愧地说道，"不完全是这样。"

他谦虚地纠正道：与席琳·迪翁的合作只是1999年格莱美颁奖典礼的一次排练。著名男高音安德烈亚·博切利——原定在广播中与加拿大超级巨星合作——无法参加排练，福斯特找来格罗班代替。"回顾过去，我认为我克服了紧张情绪，能与席琳一起演唱，"他带着笑容说道，"但我还没准备好登上主流舞台。"

然而，格罗班在那一刻展现出的才华令主持那年格莱美颁奖典礼的罗西·奥唐奈尔难以置信。"约什当时甚至还没到可以开车的年龄，"她告诉《读者文摘》杂志，"他参加了排练，我震惊了。我心想，'这个男孩是谁？歌剧少年。他像歌剧明星一样演唱！'大卫（福斯特）说，'哦，他是个年轻男孩，他将来会大有作为。'我心想，'我必须让他在我的节目中表演！'"

在罗西·奥唐奈尔秀上的表演对格罗班来说更像是一个意外。"要是能告诉你这是一个造就明星的时刻就好了，"他说，"但事实并非如此。这是罗西为我做的一件了不起的事情。这成为我一生中的一段历史。"表演后，"我回到学校。没人知道我的名字。我没有签约。没有制作人，唱片公司，公关人员，经纪人或经理。我只有我的父母。"

格罗班的成长环境虽然位于好莱坞中心，但并不被娱乐界包围。他的母亲林迪是一位视觉艺术教师，父亲杰克是一名执行招聘人员，同时精通小号演奏。家中经常播放Blood, Sweat & Tears、格蕾迪丝·奈特、埃尔顿·约翰和奥蒂斯·雷丁的音乐，以及父亲的爵士乐和古典乐专辑。儿时，格罗班还被带去观看洛杉矶版的《歌剧魅影》。"我认为这是我见过的最酷的演出，"他说，"作为一个青春期的少年，我与歌剧魅影这个反英雄息息相关。'他只是被误解了！让他弹他的风琴吧！'我发现自己为他辩护。但我会演唱这首音乐，因为它如此撕心裂肺，美得令人心碎。"

《歌剧魅影》引领格罗班接触了《星期日公园中的乔治》和其他音乐剧。"我完全着迷了，"格罗班说，"我想，'这是我适合的一种媒介。我想演唱。我想演戏。我想不跳舞——但我想做其他两件事！'"他得到了家人的全力支持。"他们希望利用他们在我身上看到的任何狂野能量，"他说，"我患有注意力缺陷多动症但不知道。我活蹦乱跳，课堂上走神。我常坐在后排，因为沉浸在自我世界中。我认为我父母将这些艺术灵感视为表达和自信的入口。"

他曾在初中首次独唱时的经历，是他人生中最大的灵感迸发："我像许多喜欢唱歌却羞于承认的年轻歌手一样，加入了合唱团。我站在后排，享受混声合唱。"但当他的合唱老师理查德·贝伦特问班上是否有人知道咯咯唱法时，格罗班——感谢父亲的爵士乐唱片——举手了。他被选中在格什温爵士乐经典曲目"太棒了"中进行咯咯唱法独唱。

尽管担心现场咯咯唱会导致社会性死亡（"这就像……死刑犯行刑，"他说），但在大约70名观众面前的演出之夜，一切都奏效了。"听到我通过麦克风演唱，没有合唱团陪伴，表达一首我喜爱的歌曲……那一刻我永远不会忘记。就像光环一样。对于一个从未专注过的孩子来说，我感觉自己正在超速公路上专注。"

更棒的是，这让演唱成为一个安全的身份认同。"在学校，即使最硬汉的孩子也说，'伙计，那太棒了，'"他说。他从"那个羞怯的、交不到朋友的孩子"变成了一个歌手。这将我们带回格莱美奖、罗西·奥唐奈尔秀，以及大约两年后的2001年5月，另一个你可能记得的主流时刻：他在《阿莉·麦比尔》中同时担任演员和歌手。然后，终于，首张同名专辑。"我能在绝对的宁静中制作一张专辑，"格罗班说，"没人知道我即将到来。"

当它在2001年11月首次发行时，"它并没有一出现就大获成功，"他说。好吧……一开始。他与夏洛特·教堂合作演唱的"祈祷"，作为2002年2月盐湖城冬季奥运会闭幕式的一部分，被估计有10亿人观看。六周后，随着势头的增长，20/20做了一个关于这位年轻明星的特辑。"我从排行榜第120位一下子上升到第20位，"他说。突破终于宣告成功。在2002年7月《纽约时报》的一篇文章中，将他称为"新男孩奇才"时，当时21岁的格罗班为自己设定了下一个大目标：百老汇。当被问及梦想中的角色时，他回答："《斯威尼·托德》中的任何角色。"

快进10年，格罗班达到了所有目标：格莱美提名、白金唱片、场场爆满的演唱会，以及一群"格罗班迷"跟随他每一次演出（有些人甚至从观众席高喊求婚）。世界为他而开。但格罗班说，他仍在探索自己。在他青春期，他最喜欢的两件事是唱歌和演戏。这位自称电影迷的格罗班探索了各种镜头前的角色，从在《办公室》中扮演安迪·伯纳德的弟弟到2018年在Netflix喜剧《好警察》中与托尼·丹扎合作主演。他扮演过混蛋（参看他在《疯狂、愚蠢、爱》中饰演艾玛·斯通的愚蠢男朋友理查德的角色）。他在《吉米·基梅尔秀》上演唱推文，并在《阳光总在菲城上空闪耀》、《公园与游憩》、《欢乐合唱团》、《美国老爸！》和《犯罪现场调查：纽约》中饰演自己。"我确实被建议不要破坏品牌，"他承认，"但这让我展示了这个形象背后是一个真实的人。我得到的许多报道都非常严肃，把我这个歌剧少年放在了高位。喜剧是让我重新站稳脚跟、回归现实的方式。"

而这种自我贬低的喜剧对他尤其有效。"这是一种让我切割自己内心魔鬼，给自己甩脸的方式，"他说，"同时也能与一些我遇到的最有趣、最聪明的人在一起。伟大歌曲的节奏与找到能让人发笑的节奏是一样的。"

他的各种才能的终极结合最终将他带到了百老汇。2016年，他首次登上百老汇，在音乐剧《娜塔莎、皮埃尔与1812年大彗星》中亮相。他饰演的忧郁的边缘人物皮埃尔为他赢得了第一个托尼奖最佳音乐剧男主角提名。然后，在21年前在《纽约时报》中称其为梦想角色的圆满时刻，他第二次担任百老汇主演，在《斯威尼·托德：弗利特街邪恶理发师》中饰演主角斯威尼·托德，并获得了第二个托尼奖提名。"我永远不会忘记我们第一次有观众的夜晚，我站在他的身后，看着他演唱'我的朋友'的第一段，"他的搭档安纳利·阿什福德说，"这首歌是一个连环杀手在对剃须刀唱歌，我能感觉到房间里的空气变化。我能感觉到观众倾身向前。"

在2000年代初，随着格罗班的明星地位上升，媒体抓住了一位音乐行业高管的评论，称他是第一个互联网明星。格罗班的年龄使他成为最新技术的天然使用者，从直播聊天到Vine视频短片。而格罗班迷们最清晰的展示了他技术驱动的社区建设力量。这些铁杆粉丝约有2万名以上，在互联网早期聚集在一起寻找社区，同样重要的是，利用他们的集体声音游说广播电台和电视节目，让他们的最爱歌手上台。但他们也支持格罗班多年来所从事的非营利和社区工作——比如与纳尔逊·曼德拉的全球运动Project 46664合作，提高人们对非洲艾滋病/艾滋病毒的认识。格罗班说，他的忠实粉丝在2005年将他们的鼓励提升到了一个新的水平。那年在一场演出中，他记得看到一群格罗班迷向舞台移动——他们带着什么。"那像是《出版商清算》式的支票，"他说，"我不知道你在哪里能得到这样的东西！"

这些粉丝告诉格罗班他们已经筹集了很长时间的钱，这是一个捐赠，供他什么时候想开始一个基金会。"我看到一些明星在同一年被粉丝群体捧杀，"他说，"而我有一群人，他们不仅与我的音乐相连，还想成为其他方面的一部分？这是我一生中最深刻的事情之一。"

格罗班将这些资金转入了后来成为"找到你的光"基金会，这是一个支持艺术教育的组织。"艺术教育不仅仅是让人感觉良好的课外活动，"他说，"它可以为其他孩子带来生命的拯救和肯定，就像对我一样。"自成立以来，该基金会已向美国450个艺术教育组织捐赠了超过750万美元。与格罗班一起担任基金会董事会成员的还有三位理解创造力对孩子生活影响的人——他的父母和弟弟克里斯。"这项慈善事业中令人惊叹的一个方面是他如何深入地将家人融入其中，"找到你的光基金会执行董事杰弗里·多林格说，"慈善事业对他来说并非虚荣项目——它根植于对艺术如何让世界更光明美好的深刻好奇。"

45岁的格罗班，人生由无数个选择组成，在他看来，自己做过的最好的决定是什么？"同意制作百老汇首秀是一个，"他说，"重温孩提时的梦想，明知道可能会失败，评论家和观众可能会说'回你的家去。'"

他停顿了一下思考。

在2026年最甜蜜的求婚中，四月份，格罗班在迪士尼乐园单膝跪地向长期交往的女友、女演员娜塔莉·麦奎恩求婚。他表示：“那大概是我这一生做出的最佳决定，问出那句问题。”他继续说道：“这也是我为自己做的决定。我一直承受着一种期待感，总觉得还有一个下一个目标。你永远不会放慢脚步，火车总在前进。而将自己放低，提出那个问题，对我来说意味着你也值得拥有这一切。这需要我给自己很大的勇气和允许。”

如今，他在推广最新专辑《Cinematic》，这张专辑收录了从《007：天幕坠落》到《时光如流》等经典电影曲目。10月份，他将在拉斯维加斯凯撒宫的科洛塞姆剧院举办5场演出驻唱。他说：“现在我比第一次走红毯时人们高喊我名字时感到更幸福。”在他看来，中年这一阶段，他拥有了更广阔的视角，经历过人生的高低起伏。

在采访中，格罗班突然哼唱起了琼妮·米切尔的《两面》，唱得恰到好处，完美地为我们的对话画上句号。他说道：“我非常理解这首歌的意思。当年17岁时，我唱这些歌时，还没有真正经历过人生。我并不知道那些情感是什么样的，也不知道任何事情。但如今，拥有了丰富的人生阅历后，再唱这些曾经的歌曲，它们承载着更深层次的意义。”

It makes total sense that Josh Groban’s new album is called Cinematic, because his origin story sounds like something out of the movies: Anxious kid struggles to focus in school, joins the choir (and turns out to be pretty great at singing), works with a vocal coach, gets in front of Grammy-winning producer David Foster and then, at the age of 17, is sharing a stage with Celine Dion. And then … fame and fortune and happily ever after, right? “Well,” says Groban with a blush, when we sit down on a warm May day in New York City, “not exactly.”

He fact-checks with a heap of modesty: The Celine Dion moment was just part of a rehearsal for the 1999 Grammys. Famed tenor Andrea Bocelli—set to duet with the Canadian superstar on the broadcast—wasn’t able to make it to practice, so Foster called Groban to stand in. “And while I think, in hindsight, I held my own through the nerves to sing with Celine,” he says with a chuckle, “I was not ready for primetime.”

But Groban’s talent in that moment, says Rosie O’Donnell, who was hosting the Grammys that year and caught the performance, was undeniable. “Josh was [basically] not old enough to drive,” she tells Reader’s Digest. “And he did the rehearsal and I was in shock. I said, ‘Who is that kid? Opera boy. He sang like an opera star!’ And David [Foster] said, ‘Oh, he’s this young kid and he’s going to go big places,’ and I’m like, ‘Well, I gotta have him on my show!’”

Singing on The Rosie O’Donnell Show not long after felt like a fluke to Groban. “I wish I could tell you that was a star-making moment,” he says, “but it wasn’t. It was an amazing thing that Rosie did for me. That’s a piece of my history.” But after the appearance, “I went back to class. Nobody knew my name. I wasn’t signed. I didn’t have a producer, a record label, a publicist, an agent or a manager. I had my parents.”

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

The beginnings

So who was that kid who had the chops to duet with Celine Dion at 17? The son of a visual arts teacher (his mom, Lindy) and an executive recruiter who happened to play a mean trumpet (his dad, Jack), Groban says he grew up “in the center of Hollywood, but not surrounded by show business.” That said, creativity was embraced and curiosity rewarded.

Groban’s home had Blood, Sweat & Tears, Gladys Knight, Elton John and Otis Redding playing on repeat, along with his dad’s jazz and classical albums. Groban was also taken to see the Los Angeles production of The Phantom of the Opera as a kid. “I thought it was the coolest show I’d ever seen in my life,” he says. “As an angsty tween, I connected with the antihero-ness of the Phantom. ‘He’s just misunderstood! Let him play his organ!’ I found myself defending him. But I’d sing the music because it was so heart-wrenching and beautiful.”

Phantom led to Sunday in the Park with George and other musicals. “I was totally hooked,” Groban says. “I was like, ‘This is a medium that I feel I’m right for. I want to sing. I want to act. I want to not dance—but I want to do the other two!’” And he did so with the full support of his family.

“They wanted to harness whatever wild energy they saw in me,” he says. “I had ADHD and didn’t know it. I was bouncing off the walls. I was distracted in class. I was sitting in the back a lot because I was lost inside myself. And I think my parents saw these artistic bursts of inspiration as an access point for expression and confidence.”

The biggest burst, he says, came from his first solo moment on stage in junior high: “I did what a lot of young singers do when they love it but are too shy to say they love it, which is: I joined the choir. I’d be in the back and just loved the blend.” But when his choral teacher Richard Berent asked the class if anyone knew what scat singing was, Groban—thanks to his dad’s jazz records—raised his hand. He was then chosen to scat a solo in the Gershwin jazz standard “’S Wonderful.”

Though he worried a live scat would equate to social suicide (“It was like … dead man walking,” he says), on the night of the performance, with about 70 people in the audience, everything clicked. “Hearing myself on a microphone with no choir behind me, expressing a song that I loved … that was a moment that I’ll never forget. It was like a halo of light. For a kid that was never focused, I felt like I was on this superhighway of focus.”

Even better? It made singing a safe identity to embrace. “In school, even the hardest-edged kids were like, ‘Yeah, bro, that was great,’” he says. He went from being “the shy kid that can’t make friends” to something different: a singer.

The (long-awaited) breakthrough

And that brings us back to the Grammys, The Rosie O’Donnell Show and then, about two years later, in May 2001, another mainstream moment you might remember: a role both acting and singing on Ally McBeal. From there, finally, the self-titled first album.

“I got to make an album in absolute peace and quiet,” Groban says. “Nobody knew I was on the horizon.” And when it debuted in November 2001, “It did not come out of the gate successful,” he says. Well … at first. His duet with Charlotte Church, singing “The Prayer” as part of the Salt Lake City Winter Olympics closing ceremony in February 2002, was seen by an estimated 1 billion people.

And six weeks later, as the momentum was building, 20/20 did a feature on the young star. “I went from 120 on the charts to, like, 20 the next day,” he says. The breakthrough was finally official. In a New York Times piece in July of that year minting him “The New Boy Wonder,” the then-21-year-old put his stake in the ground for his next big goal: Broadway. When asked about his dream part, he answered, “Any role in Sweeney Todd.”

The pivots

Fast-forward 10 years, and Groban had hit all the marks: Grammy nominations, platinum records, packed arena shows and a fan army of “Grobanites” flocking to every appearance (some shouting marriage proposals from the stands). The world was his oyster.

But Groban was still, he says, figuring himself out. (And remember that in his teens, the two things he loved to do were singing and acting.) The self-described film geek explored all kinds of on-camera roles, from popping up as Andy Bernard’s younger brother in two episodes of The Office to co-leading the Netflix comedy The Good Cop with Tony Danza in 2018.

He played jerks (see his still-discussed role as Emma Stone’s lame boyfriend Richard in Crazy, Stupid, Love). He sang tweets on Jimmy Kimmel Live! and played himself on It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, Parks and Recreation, Glee, American Dad! and CSI: NY.

“I was advised for sure to not blow the brand,” he admits. “But it allowed me to show that there was a human being behind this persona. A lot of the press I got was so serious and so much like, ‘We’re putting this opera child on a pedestal.’ Comedy was my way to get back on my feet, back on the ground.”

And that turned out to be especially true for self-deprecating comedy. “It was a way for me to machete through my own demons, put a pie in my own face,” he says. “And also to be around some of the funniest, smartest people that I’ve ever met. The rhythm of a great song is the same as finding the rhythm that makes somebody laugh.”

The ultimate team-up of his talents finally led Groban to Broadway. He appeared there in 2016 for the first time in the musical Natasha, Pierre & The Great Comet of 1812. His leading role as depressed outcast Pierre earned him his first Tony Award nomination for Best Actor in a Musical.

Then, in a full-circle moment, 21 years after calling it his dream role in the New York Times, his second Broadway starring role was the titular role of Sweeney Todd in Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, for which he got his second Tony nod.

“I’ll never forget our first night with an audience, and I was standing behind him watching him sing the first verse of “My Friend,” says his co-star Annaleigh Ashford. “The song is a serial killer singing to a razor blade, and I could feel the air in the room change. I could feel the audience lean in.”

The impact

Back in the early 2000s, as Groban’s star was rising, the media clasped onto a quote from a music industry exec who called him the first internet star. Groban’s youth made him a natural for the latest technologies, from live chats to Vine video shorts. And the clearest example of his technology-fueled community-building power is the influence of the Grobanites.

These diehards, estimated at over 20,000  strong, came together in the early days of the web to find community and, just as importantly, leverage their collective voice to lobby radio stations and TV programs to get their favorite singer on the air. But they also supported the nonprofit and community work that Groban has embraced over the years—like working with Project 46664, Nelson Mandela’s global campaign to raise awareness of HIV/AIDS in Africa.

Groban says his devoted fans took their encouragement to a new level in 2005. During a show that year, he recalls, he saw a group of Grobanites make a move toward the stage—and they had something with them. “It was one of those Publisher’s Clearinghouse–type checks,” he says. “I don’t even know where you get one of those!”

The fans told Groban they’d been raising the money for a long time and that it was a donation for whenever he wanted to start a foundation. “I see artists who are built up and torn down in the same year by fan bases,” he says. “And for me to have a group of people that connects with my music but also wants to be a part of the rest of it as well? That’s one of the most profound things that’s ever happened to me.”

Groban channeled the funding into what became the Find Your Light Foundation, an organization that supports arts education. “Arts education isn’t just a feel-good extracurricular,” he says. “It can be as lifesaving and life affirming for other kids as it was for me.” Since its inception, the foundation has donated over $7.5 million to 450 arts education organizations around the United States. Joining Groban on the foundation’s board are three people who understand the power of creativity in kids’ lives—his parents and his brother, Chris.

“An amazing part of this philanthropic journey is how deeply he involves his family,” says Find Your Light Foundation Executive Director Jeffrey Dollinger. “Philanthropy isn’t a vanity project for him—it’s rooted in a deep curiosity of how the arts can make the world a brighter and better place.”

The future

At 45, with a life consisting of a billion individual choices thus far, what does Groban see as the best decision he ever made? “Saying yes to making a Broadway debut was a big one,” he says. “Revisiting a dream that I’d had since I was a kid, knowing full well that it could go sideways and the critics and audiences could say ‘Go back to your home.’”

He pauses to think. “And proposing.”

We haven’t yet talked about the sweetest marriage proposal of 2026: In April, Groban got down on one knee in Disneyland to propose to his longtime girlfriend, actress Natalie McQueen. “That’s probably the best decision I’ve ever made in my life, asking that question,” he says. “It was also a decision for myself. I’ve carried this feeling of expectation. There’s always something next. You’re never slowing down; the train just keeps moving. And to get down on one knee and ask that question to me was like, Right, you also deserve this. It took a lot for me to finally give myself that permission.” He smiles.

McQueen is by his side now as he tours his latest album, Cinematic, an eclectic collection of movie classics, from Skyfall to As Time Goes By. In October, he’ll perform a five-show residency at The Colosseum at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas.

“I’m feeling more blessed now than I ever felt during that first red carpet when everybody was shouting [my] name,” he says. At this midlife mark, he says, he has a better perspective. He’s been through both the highs and the lows. (At this point of the interview, Groban jumps into the chorus of Joni Mitchell’s “Both Sides Now”—and, of course, it’s wonderful. The exact right choice for the closing credits of our conversation.)

“I relate to that song very much,” he says. “When I first sang some of these songs at 17, I hadn’t lived. I didn’t know what that stuff felt like. I didn’t know anything. So to have all of that rich nuance of life behind me now, to sing all the songs in my catalog now—it comes from a much deeper place.”

凭借《印第安纳琼斯：魔鬼之城》的Short Round和《怪兽小子》的Data，凯·昆·黄（Ke Huy Quan）首次征服了观众的心。然而，在饰演这两个经典角色之后，他忽然从影坛消失。多年后，他以《万物皆有尽头》中的Waymond Wang重新回归，并凭借这一角色斩获奥斯卡、金球奖和美国演员工会奖最佳男配角奖项。2023年，他还被《时代》杂志评选为全球最具影响力人物之一。自此，他不仅在《雷神洛基》中现身，还在《爱情伤人》中展现了惊人的战斗力，并为《疯狂动物城2》献声。

现在，凯·昆·黄以更加个人化的方式带领我们回顾他的传奇经历——他的首本自传《永不言弃》（*Never Say Die*）本月出版。这本书追溯了他从难民营里的孩子到奥斯卡舞台上的明星的成长历程。然而，凯·昆·黄告诉《读者文摘》，这本书的核心并非有关他的辉煌时刻，而是那些被遗忘的岁月。他说：“那些是最难写的篇章，因为它们非常私人。”这大约是30年的“寂静期”，许多人以为他已经消失了。

在《读者文摘·升降机访谈》（*The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview*）的这一期中，我们与凯·昆·黄深入探讨了《永不言弃》的创作过程。他揭秘了回忆最艰难的章节时的心路历程，透露了写作时的零食选择，并回答了粉丝最关心的问题。他说：“粉丝总是想知道《印第安纳琼斯》和《怪兽小子》的幕后故事，以及与哈里森·福特合作的感受。如果你是这两部电影的粉丝，你会喜欢这些章节。”当被问及他的理想晚宴嘉宾时，他毫不犹豫地提到了《怪兽小子》的同伴、多年的好友杰夫·科恩（Jeff Cohen）。

请继续阅读我们与凯·昆·黄的独家访谈，并在下方探索他的推荐读物！

**关于《读者文摘》**
《读者文摘》已有超过100年的历史，一直致力于分享最好的书籍。我们曾与许多畅销书作者合作，包括苏珊·奥利安（Susan Orlean）、珍妮特·伊万诺维奇（Janet Evanovich）和亚历克斯·黑利（Alex Haley），后者的普利策奖获奖作品《根》最初是由《读者文摘》资助和出版的。通过《读者文摘书评》（原名《精选篇章》和《缩略版小说》），我们已出版了各种精选小说合集。我们与许多顶尖小说家合作，包括詹姆斯·帕特森（James Patterson）、露丝·韦尔（Ruth Ware）、克里斯汀·汉娜（Kristin Hannah）等。由图书编辑特蕾西·奈瑟科特（Tracey Neithercott）主持的《读者文摘书俱乐部》向读者介绍了更多当代最佳小说，包括新锐作者、畅销书作家和获奖作家的作品。本文由莱·贝尔兹·雷（Leigh Belz Ray）采访凯·昆·黄。我们核查所有事实和数据，确保它们准确可靠，并定期更新以保持时效性。了解更多关于我们的团队、贡献者以及编辑政策的信息。

articles.summary:
If anyone knows a thing or two about never saying die, it’s Ke Huy Quan. The actor first stole hearts as Short Round in Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and Data in The Goonies, and then, after decades away from acting, he made the kind of Hollywood comeback that movies are made of with Everything Everywhere All at Once. His unforgettable turn as Waymond Wang earned him an Academy Award, Golden Globe and SAG Award for Best Supporting Actor, and in 2023, Time named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world. Since then, he’s popped up in Loki, kicked some serious butt in Love Hurts and lent his voice to Zootopia 2.

Now, Quan is taking us somewhere even more personal: inside his own remarkable story with Never Say Die, his first book, released this month. The memoir traces his journey from a child in a refugee camp to a beloved actor on the Oscars stage, but Quan tells Reader’s Digest that its real heart lies in the decades when Hollywood stopped calling. “Those were the hardest chapters to write because they’re super personal,” he says of the roughly 30 “quiet years” when many people thought he had simply disappeared.

For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, we caught up with Quan to dive deeper into Never Say Die—and, in true Escalator Interview fashion, we couldn’t resist getting a little nosy along the way. He opened up about what it was like revisiting some of the most difficult chapters of his life, revealed his writing snack of choice and answered the big question he knows you’re wondering about. “[Fans] always want to know what it’s like making Indiana Jones and The Goonies, and what it was like working with Harrison Ford,” Quan says. “If you’re fans of those two movies, you’ll love those chapters.” And when it came time to assemble his dream dinner party? Let’s just say fellow Goonie and longtime friend Jeff Cohen definitely has a seat at the table.
